Primary vs Secondary Market: IPO, FPO, Rights Issue and QIP

New securities are sold in the primary market, and existing ones are traded in the secondary market. This guide compares the two and sets out each way a company can raise money.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

Primary and secondary market compared

BasisPrimary marketSecondary market
What is soldNew securitiesExisting securities
Who gets the moneyThe company (or selling shareholders in an offer for sale)The selling investor
PriceSet by the company or through book buildingSet by supply and demand
PurposeRaising capitalLiquidity and price discovery
ExampleApplying in an IPOBuying a listed share on NSE

Ways of raising capital

  • IPO: the first sale of shares to the public, after which the company is listed.
  • FPO: a further public issue by a listed company.
  • Rights issue: new shares offered to existing shareholders, usually at a discount, in proportion to what they hold.
  • Bonus issue: free shares from reserves. It raises no money, so it is not really a way of raising capital, although students often group it with these.
  • Private placement: shares or bonds sold to a selected small group of investors.
  • QIP: a quick share sale by a listed company to qualified institutional buyers.
  • Preferential allotment: shares issued to chosen investors, such as promoters or a strategic partner.

The IPO process step by step

  • The company appoints merchant bankers, also called book-running lead managers.
  • It files a DRHP with SEBI, setting out its business, finances, risks and use of the money.
  • SEBI reviews it and gives its observations.
  • The company files the red herring prospectus and announces a price band.
  • Investors bid through ASBA over the issue period; anchor investors commit a day before.
  • The final price and the allotment are set based on demand.
  • Shares reach demat accounts and start trading on the exchange.

Fresh issue and offer for sale

An IPO can have two parts. In a fresh issue, the company creates new shares and gets the money. In an offer for sale (OFS), existing shareholders sell their holdings and the money goes to them, not the company. Checking this split in the prospectus tells you how much money will actually go into the business.

Fixed price and book building

In a fixed-price issue, the price is announced in advance and demand is known only at the close. In book building, investors bid within a price band, demand is visible daily, and the final price comes from the bids. Almost all large Indian IPOs now use book building.

Investor categories in an IPO

  • QIB: qualified institutional buyers such as mutual funds and insurers.
  • NII: non-institutional investors, which includes HNIs applying above the retail limit.
  • RII: retail individual investors applying up to the retail limit, ₹2 lakh at present.

Exam and interview questions

What is the main difference between the primary and secondary market?

In the primary market, securities are issued for the first time and money goes to the issuer. In the secondary market, investors trade existing securities with each other.

What is book building?

A method of price discovery in which investors bid within a price band, and the final issue price is fixed according to the demand.

What is the difference between an IPO and an FPO?

An IPO is a company's first public share sale. An FPO is a later public sale by a company that is already listed.

What is a green shoe option?

An over-allotment option that lets the company issue extra shares if demand is strong. The money is used to stabilise the price after listing.
